method_card.title: How to Solve Linear Inequalities
method_card.content:
Solve inequalities like equations, with one key rule: flip the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative.

Number line: Open circle for < or >, filled circle for \(\leq\) or \(\geq\).

Double inequalities: e.g. \(3 < 2x + 1 \leq 9\). Solve all parts at once.

bronze.hint: Subtract 4 from both sides to get x on its own.

misconceptions.message: Take 4 off both sides, do not add it: x > 9 − 4 = 5.
You have the right boundary, but the arrow points the wrong way. x > 5 means x is bigger than 5.
To undo 2 times x, divide by 2, do not multiply: x < 10 ÷ 2 = 5.
The boundary 5 is right, but the arrow is reversed. Dividing by a positive keeps the same symbol.
To undo 2 times x, divide by 2, do not subtract 2: x < 5.
Add 3 to both sides, do not subtract it: x ≥ 7 + 3 = 10.
The boundary 10 is right, but the arrow points the wrong way.
The question uses ≥, so 10 is included. x > 10 wrongly leaves 10 out.

Take 7 off both sides, do not add it: x < 3 − 7 = −4.
The boundary −4 is right, but the arrow points the wrong way.
3 − 7 = −4, not 4. The answer is negative.

problem_bank.silver_description: Negatives requiring a sign flip, and double inequalities
problem_bank.gold_description: Fractional and bracketed inequalities, integer solutions, combined inequalities

bronze.title: Bronze: one and two step inequalities
steps: Solve an inequality just like an equation. Undo the + or − first, then the × or ÷.
Do the same thing to both sides, and keep the same symbol the whole way through.
Your answer is a range, like \(x > 3\): every number bigger than 3, not a single value.

silver.title: Silver: negatives and double inequalities
steps: If you divide or multiply by a negative, flip the sign, so \(<\) becomes \(>\).
For a double inequality like \(1 < 2x \leq 8\), do the same step to all three parts.
A strict symbol (\(<\)) leaves the boundary out; \(\leq\) keeps it in.

gold.title: Gold: integer solutions and combined inequalities
steps: Rearrange to a range first, then list every integer inside it, negatives included.
Watch each end: a strict symbol excludes the boundary, \(\leq\) or \(\geq\) includes it.
For two separate inequalities, solve each, then combine them into one overlapping range.

steps.say: A puzzle first, no algebra needed. A £20 hoodie: you have £8 saved and add £4 every week.

steps.pre: Fewest whole weeks until you can afford it?
steps.hint: You need £12 more and save £4 each week.

steps.say: 3 weeks works, and so do 4, 5, and up. The answer is a whole range, 3 or more, not one number. Writing your savings as \(8 + 4w\), you found where \(8 + 4w \geq 20\). That is an inequality: solve it like an equation, but the answer is a range.

steps.pre: Check the boundary: after exactly 3 weeks, how much have you saved, in £?
steps.hint: Start at £8 and add £4 three times.

steps.say: £20, exactly enough. That boundary is where \(8 + 4w = 20\), and the inequality says 3 weeks or more. One warning for later: if you ever divide by a negative, the inequality sign flips over.
Solve \(4x + 3 < 19\) the same way you solve an equation. First take 3 off both sides.
So \(4x < 16\). Now divide both sides by 4.
So \(x < 4\): every number less than 4. Keep the same symbol, \(<\), because we did not divide by a negative.

steps.done: 15 is less than 19, so x = 3 fits.
19 is not less than 19, so 4 is NOT included. That is why its circle is open.

steps.say: Solve \(3 - 2x \leq 9\). Take 3 off both sides first.
So \(-2x \leq 6\). Now divide by −2. Because we divide by a NEGATIVE, the sign flips: \(\leq\) becomes \(\geq\).

steps.hint: A positive divided by a negative is negative.

steps.say: So \(x \geq -3\). The flip is the whole point: dividing by a negative reverses the arrow.

steps.done: 3 is less than 9, so x = 0 fits, matching x ≥ −3.
11 is not ≤ 9, so −4 fails. The arrow really does point the other way.

steps.say: How many integers satisfy \(-2 \leq 3x + 4 < 13\)? Do the same step to all three parts. First subtract 4 from each part.
So \(-6 \leq 3x < 9\). Divide all three parts by 3.
So \(-2 \leq x < 3\). List the integers, negatives included. −2 is in (\(\leq\)), 3 is out (\(<\)).

steps.done: Five integers. The trap is forgetting −2 and −1.
